title: One deed tips the world (3:4)
hook: see yourself and the world as evenly balanced; your next deed could tip it
tomorrow: what is the shofar actually trying to say?

segments.voice: Yesterday: even after death. The conversation ends, the return doesn't have to. Today Maimonides jumps to chapter three, and from one grave to the whole world.

Field day, tug-of-war. The rope has gone dead still, both sides straining, nobody moving. Then one kid at the very back digs in their heels, and the whole thing slides. Can one small deed really tip the whole world? Maimonides says, in effect, yes, and the puzzle is how he gets there. He tells every person to see themselves as exactly half innocent and half guilty, all year long. And the whole world, too: exactly half and half. Every person, every day, perfectly even? That can't be a headcount.
screen: `THE ROPE GOES STILL.` → `HALF INNOCENT, HALF GUILTY.` → `THE WHOLE WORLD, TOO?`

segments.voice: It isn't. Read what comes next and the puzzle solves itself. If a person does one wrong, he writes, they tip themselves and the whole world toward guilt, and bring ruin. If they do one mitzvah, one good deed, they tip themselves and the whole world toward merit, and bring rescue. So the half-and-half isn't a report on anyone's record. It's a way of standing. Picture the scale perfectly level, and suddenly your next act isn't small. It's the one that decides. A person who thinks they're mostly good can coast. A person who thinks they're mostly bad can give up. Maimonides takes both excuses away with one picture: the scale is always even, and it's always your move. He finds it in Proverbs: "the righteous is an everlasting foundation." He reads it as the one whose single good deed tipped the world and saved it. The idea is older than him; the Talmud says something close, that a person should see themselves as half and half. Notice he isn't promising you'll see the result. Nobody gets to watch the scale. You just act as if this deed is the one. One deed tips the world.
screen: `NOT A HEADCOUNT.` · `ONE WRONG, ONE MITZVAH.` · `NO COASTING, NO GIVING UP.` · `AN EVERLASTING FOUNDATION.` · then, large: `ONE DEED TIPS THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a sticky note or scrap of paper. Write one small good deed you could do today, and when: a call, a dish washed, a thank-you sent. Set it where you'll see it, then sit with the scale in your mind, perfectly level, waiting on you.
One deed tips the world: Maimonides' picture of a scale held perfectly even, so that your next act, good or bad, is the one that decides.
screen: `ONE DEED TIPS THE WORLD — today's word`.

segments.voice: For the road: one deed tips the world, and the scale is level, waiting on your move. That's day fifteen forty-nine.

screen: `DAY 1549 COUNTS.` → `MAIMONIDES, THE LAWS OF RETURN · 12 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT IS THE SHOFAR ACTUALLY TRYING TO SAY?`

howItsDone: Some Jews take on an extra mitzvah or a little more tzedakah in the days around Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, drawing on Maimonides' picture of the evenly balanced scale.

Maimonides' reading of Proverbs 10:25 ('this one tipped the world and saved it'): confirm.
